How to install BackDown, how it works, step-by-step guides, and every command. BackDown indexes your drives, finds what's duplicated across all of them, and tells you, with a SHA-256 hash behind every claim, which drives are safe to wipe. It recognises what things are and where they came from, files old drives into one archive, keeps mirrors, watches your drives' health, and gets files back from failing or emptied drives. It runs on your own computer and only ever reads the drives it looks at, except when you ask it to copy into an archive, keep a mirror, or free up a drive. New here? Start with Getting started : install it, open it, index two drives, see what's duplicated, and ask whether a drive is safe to wipe. Concepts explains the ideas the rest of the docs rely on. Note These docs describe BackDown 1.0.0-beta.1: the desktop app, its background service and the backdown command, on Linux, macOS and Windows. It's a beta, so some things will change before 1.0; the status page has what's released and what's next.

Drives and scans, fast rescans, the time slider, hashes and proof, what "safe to wipe" means, copies across file systems, recognised things and where they came from, the background service, and drive health. The ideas the rest of the docs rely on. Each section says what BackDown does, and what it doesn't.

A root is a drive, or a top-level folder, that you've indexed: /media/old-drive , /mnt/nas , E:\ . BackDown calls it a drive and names it after the last part of its path ( old-drive ). Roots can't be nested inside each other: index each drive or top-level folder once. BackDown knows a root by its path. Plug a drive back in where it was mounted before and BackDown carries on with it; mounted somewhere else, it's a new root. A root whose folder is missing, or empty although it held files, counts as not connected: its files aren't read, and they wait for it. Indexing stays on one file system unless you pass --cross-filesystems , so a drive's scan doesn't wander into other drives mounted inside it. Symbolic links are neither followed nor recorded. backdown volumes lists every disk and partition on the computer (model, serial number, file system, label, where it's mounted), says what BackDown can do with each (mountable, mounted, system, encrypted, part of a volume group, swap, empty), and marks the ones the index covers. It only reads, and needs no administrator rights. Activity's "Connected drives" shows the same, with Index this on each mounted one. Mounting drives read-only A drive has to be mounted, as a folder, before it can be indexed. BackDown can mount one for you, always read-only and always as you, through the system's own tools: backdown mount /dev/sdb1 # a partition volumes calls mountable backdown mount /media/archive/Images/old-laptop.img # a disk image backdown mount # what BackDown has mounted backdown unmount /dev/sdb1 Copy System Partitions Disk images Linux udisks ( udisksctl mount -o ro ), for file systems this computer has a driver or helper for attached read-only as a loop device, then each partition mounted read-only macOS diskutil mount readOnly hdiutil attach -readonly Windows not offered: Windows can't mount a drive read-only in general, and BackDown reads drives where they are ISO, VHD and VHDX, with Mount-DiskImage -Access ReadOnly On Linux, BackDown checks the mount really is read-only and undoes it if not. It doesn't mount the running system's partitions, encrypted volumes that are still locked (unlock them in your file manager first; the unlocked volume can then be mounted), members of LVM or RAID sets, swap, or partitions with nothing recognisable on them. Where your system wants an administrator's password to mount, BackDown says so and shows the command, which asks for it itself. unmount only unmounts what BackDown mounted; detaching an image unmounts everything that was mounted from it. In the browser, Activity's "Connected drives" has Mount read-only and Unmount , and a disk image whose file systems BackDown can't read itself (XFS, btrfs, HFS+, APFS and others) offers Mount read-only too.

Every backdown index run records a scan of each root: every file's path, size and modification time, and on Linux and macOS its device and inode, so hardlinks are recognised. The files' contents aren't read while scanning. When you index a drive again: a file with the same path, size and modification time is unchanged, and keeps everything known about it, hashes included; a changed file gets a new version, and the old one is kept; a file that's gone is marked gone, and its last version is kept. A renamed or moved file counts as gone at the old path and new at the new one. A scan that's interrupted doesn't count; run the command again. Because every version is kept, the browser can show any folder as it was at any scan: that's the time slider at the bottom of a drive with two scans or more. An old version can be opened while its exact bytes still exist somewhere indexed, either the file itself, unchanged, or an identical copy (same SHA-256) on an indexed drive. Otherwise the index still remembers its size, dates and hash, but the bytes are gone. Hashing after each scan keeps that fingerprint; the background service does it for you. If a drive that held files is suddenly empty, index refuses to record it: usually the drive isn't plugged in and you're looking at its empty mount point. If it really was emptied, pass --allow-empty . Fast rescans A scan doesn't always have to open every folder. There are three ways to make one: Way What it reads Where Walk every folder everywhere; always the first scan of a drive Change log only the files and folders the drive's own record of changes names since the last scan Windows: the USN journal of NTFS drives, without administrator rights. macOS: the change history (FSEvents) of APFS and HFS+ drives File table NTFS's master file table, from start to end, instead of folder by folder Windows, when BackDown runs as administrator. Linux, for NTFS drives mounted with ntfs-3g, when your account can read the drive's device An unchanged drive with millions of files is rescanned from its change log in seconds. Linux keeps no change log for drives, so rescans there walk, or read an NTFS drive's file table. Whichever way a scan is made, it records exactly what walking every folder would, because proof needs every file. BackDown walks instead whenever there's any doubt: the change log was reset, lost its oldest entries, belongs to another drive, left something out, or says anything that doesn't add up. And it walks anyway every tenth scan, or when the last walk is 30 days old, which catches changes made where nothing was recording them (the drive plugged into another computer). index prints how each drive was scanned and why; Activity shows it under each drive's last scan. Settings > Scanning turns the change log and file table off, or changes how often to walk anyway. backdown index --method walk always walks, and --method journal or --method table use that way or fail, saying why ( when a rescan walks ).

Every claim BackDown makes about copies rests on SHA-256: two files are the same when their SHA-256 hashes are the same. Hashing everything would mean reading every byte on every drive, so hashing goes in three tiers: Size. A file whose size no other file shares can't have a duplicate, and is never read. Sample. For the rest, a quick fingerprint: the size, plus 64 KiB from the start, the middle and the end of the file. Files up to 192 KiB are read whole here, which gives their full hash straight away. Full SHA-256. Only files whose sizes and samples still match another file's are read completely. Hardlinks are one file: they're read once, and never count as each other's copy (on Linux and macOS; see below for Windows). Hashing runs one reader per drive ( --jobs 1 , right for spinning disks; raise it for SSDs, or in Settings > Hashing). Files on drives that aren't connected wait for them. A file that can't be read is marked unreadable and skipped until backdown hash --retry-errors ; one that changed since it was indexed asks you to index again. dupes , check and the background service run hash for you. The hash is SHA-256 throughout.

backdown check PATH says a drive (or a folder) is safe to wipe when every file in it has an identical copy outside it: another file with the same full SHA-256, outside PATH (a copy inside the drive you want to wipe doesn't count), and not just a hardlink to the same file. Files that couldn't be read block the verdict, because nobody knows what's in them. Empty files don't count against a drive. A file without a full hash counts as unique. check hashes everything that could have a copy first, so that only happens when no other file could be identical, or when its look-alikes are on drives that have never been connected while hashing. The verdict is about the index. A copy on a drive that isn't plugged in still counts, and a copy that went missing since its drive was last scanned would still count too. That's why freeing up a drive doesn't trust the verdict alone: before deleting a file, it reads the file and its copy again and compares them. A copy on another machine counts too, more strictly: only by SHA-256, only if that machine confirmed it within the last 7 days (a setting), and, before freeing up relies on it, only after that machine has read it again. check says how much of the verified part is only on another machine. check exits with 0 when the path is safe to wipe and 2 when files must be copied first, and lists the folders holding what exists only there ( --list names the largest 20,000 files).

Copying into an archive, to a mirror, or out of a rescue moves files between drives that don't all follow the same rules. BackDown copies the bytes, checks them, and says what it had to change: Names that would clash. Before copying, BackDown tests what the destination treats as the same name ( Photo.jpg and photo.jpg on a Mac or Windows drive, or two Unicode spellings of café ) and which names it can't hold at all (on Windows, FAT and exFAT: : , ? , * and the like, trailing dots and spaces, names such as CON or NUL ). The first name keeps its spelling and the others become photo (2).jpg ; characters the drive can't hold become - , and reserved names get _ in front. Every renaming is written to the journal, and apply lists them. Freeing up with --move-to keeps names as they are: a file that would clash with a different one is left in place. What else a file carries. On a Mac, extended attributes (resource forks, Finder info, tags) are copied and checked; a drive that can't hold them gets ._ files. On Windows, NTFS alternate data streams are copied and read back, except the "downloaded from the internet" mark ( Zone.Identifier ), which is left behind on purpose. Linux's extended attributes aren't carried, and neither are permissions, owners or ACLs anywhere: a copy gets the original's modification time. When something couldn't be kept, the journal says what, and freeing up with --move-to leaves that file where it is. Streams count for proof. On Windows, BackDown records each file's alternate data streams when it indexes (their names and sizes; they aren't part of the file's size or hash), shows them in the details pane, and only counts a copy as proof for freeing up if it has the same ones. Long paths. On Windows, paths longer than 260 characters, and names ending in a dot or a space, are read as they are. As administrator. Run as administrator on Windows, BackDown can read (never write) files your account otherwise couldn't, such as other users' folders on an old drive. Online-only files. On Windows, cloud placeholders (OneDrive and the like, whose contents aren't on the drive) are never read, because reading one would download it onto the drive. They're indexed, count as unreadable, and so keep a drive from being "safe to wipe". On a Mac, iCloud Drive's online-only ("dataless") files are left alone the same way. Hardlinks on Windows count as separate files: dupes counts the space they share as reclaimable. Copies are made the fastest way the destination allows: on btrfs, XFS and APFS as clones that share the source's blocks until one changes, on Linux otherwise by the kernel, and elsewhere by reading and writing. Every copy is then read back and compared with the source's SHA-256 before it counts; on Linux BackDown first asks the system to forget the copy it has in memory, so the read comes from the disk (elsewhere it may come from the system's cache).

BackDown recognises what things are, from the names and layout of files and folders: mail stores and Maildir mailboxes, Dovecot mdbox and sdbox stores, Thunderbird profiles, Nextcloud data, Time Machine backups, iPhone and Android backups, operating systems, Mac, Linux and Windows home folders, websites, git repositories, database dumps, disk images, photo, music and video libraries, data exports (Google Takeout, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, LinkedIn), downloads piles and recovered files. Each comes with its size, the years its files span and, where it's less than sure, how sure it is. Some are looked at more closely, still without reading anyone's messages: Dovecot mdbox and sdbox: the mailboxes and their names and, with the drive connected, message counts from Dovecot's index headers and the oldest and newest message's dates. Thunderbird profiles: which folders are copies of server mail (IMAP) and which are kept only here (Local Folders, POP), each mailbox file with its size and, with the drive connected, the accounts, addresses and servers from prefs.js . Time Machine: HFS+ backup sets ( Backups.backupdb ), APFS backups from macOS 11 on (the dated snapshot folders), and network backup bundles, with the computer, the number of snapshots and the span. BackDown doesn't mount snapshots or open the bundles. Folders that programs can make again are flagged as regenerable : caches, thumbnails, node_modules , build output, virtual environments, trash and the like (Settings > Junk rules lists them, and takes your own). They still count: a drive is only safe to wipe when they have copies too. A filing plan can leave them out, and then they stay on the old drive when you free it up. It also works out where things came from, and when, by reading small files on connected drives: Source What it says Backup scripts ( rsync , scp , rclone , cp -a , robocopy , tar ) Copied from which machine, with which tool, from which script iPhone backups' Info.plist Backed up from which device, which model, on which day Time Machine folder names and records Backed up from which computer, last on which day /etc/hostname , /etc/os-release Which machine a system disk was, which system git configuration A clone of which remote, on which branch GNU ddrescue map files Rescued from which device Database dump headers Dumped from which host, on which day Sync markers Kept in sync by Syncthing, Resilio Sync, Dropbox, Nextcloud or ownCloud Only small files are read (scripts up to 256 KiB, plists up to 8 MiB), and only on drives that are connected. backdown entities lists what's recognised; the background service recognises each drive again after it's been scanned and hashed.

backdown overlaps shows how much of each drive, top-level folder and recognised thing already exists elsewhere, and where most of it is: "89% elsewhere: 89% on archive". It's the same SHA-256 test as check , summed up per place. The report and the filing plan use it to find what's already archived.

backdown daemon is BackDown running in the background; the app starts it, and backdown service install keeps it running. It: rescans each drive when it's due (every 24 hours unless Settings says otherwise; --rescan-every 12h , or never ), and as soon as a drive that was away comes back; hashes after every scan, then recognises what changed; serves the browser on 127.0.0.1 (port 8787), with a private link that backdown open and backdown app open; runs one job at a time, so the index has one writer and each drive one reader; rescues and syncs with other machines run beside the other jobs; reads every drive's health every six hours and tells you when one gets worse; keeps each mirror in sync and checked, and, if you turned it on, looks for updates once a day. It's stopped safely at any point: jobs commit as they go and carry on where they stopped. backdown service install runs it for you, as you, with no extra rights: a systemd user service on Linux, a LaunchAgent on macOS, and a scheduled task that starts it when you log on on Windows. On Linux, sudo backdown service install --system runs it for the whole machine instead (a NAS or a server): as a backdown user that can read every file and write none, sandboxed by systemd, with no network beyond this computer. Members of the backdown group can use it. The machine-wide service only reads: it never wipes, rescues, tidies or mounts, and doesn't reach other machines. While a daemon is running, it owns the index. index , hash , dupes , check , scans , status , health , remote sync and apply --go are handed to it, and your terminal follows the progress; wipe , dedup and mail merge check first, then hand the work to it. --local makes a command use the index directly. On Windows, terminal commands always use the index directly: the browser is how you talk to the service there.

Drives say how they're doing, through SMART: sectors they've had to replace or can't read, cable errors, wear on SSDs, temperature, and their own verdict. BackDown reads what each physical drive will tell an ordinary account: through udisks on Linux (and smartctl where your account may use it), diskutil (and smartctl if it's installed) on macOS, and Windows' storage cmdlets, which share their counters only with an administrator. A drive's verdict is ok , warning , failing or unknown (no health data). Readings are kept in the index under the drive's serial number, so its history follows it from port to port. backdown health shows every drive and exits with 2 when a connected one is failing; the background service reads them every six hours and when a drive appears, and tells you when one gets worse. Drive health has the details, including what each system can and can't read.

Delete only what has a verified copy elsewhere, move what exists only on the drive first, and see exactly what will happen before anything does. Freeing up a drive is the one thing BackDown deletes, and only when you ask. The rule is simple: a file is deleted only when an identical copy exists outside what you're freeing, and both have just been read again and compared. What exists only on the drive can be moved somewhere first, or left where it is. It works on whole drives or on folders, so it also cleans up duplicates: free up the copy you don't want, and the one you keep is its proof. Freeing up is marked Pro; in this beta everything is unlocked ( Free and Pro ). backdown check , which says whether a drive is safe to wipe, is free.
1. Index everything that might hold copies

The copies have to be in the index. Index the drive you want to free and the drives that should hold its copies, then check it: backdown index /media/old-drive /media/archive backdown check /media/old-drive Copy check hashes what's needed and gives the verdict: SAFE TO WIPE , or COPY FIRST with the folders holding what exists nowhere else ( what "safe to wipe" means ). You don't need "safe to wipe" to go on, as long as you decide what happens to the rest.

Without --go , backdown wipe only shows what it would do: backdown wipe /media/old-drive Copy /media/old-drive 44 files, 182 MB 162 MB has an identical copy elsewhere: 99 MB in archive/Media, 60 MB in archive/Backups, 3 MB in archive/Documents 20 MB (7 files) exists only here: left in place (--move-to <folder> moves it first) Nothing was changed. To wipe: backdown wipe "/media/old-drive" --go --confirm "old-drive" Every file is re-read before it's deleted, and so is its copy (--trust-index skips that). Copy You can name several drives or folders at once. Copies inside what you've named don't count: they're going too.
3. Decide what happens to the files that exist only there

Either leave them, and they stay on the drive, or move them first with --move-to : backdown wipe /media/old-drive --move-to /media/archive/Unsorted Copy Each is copied to <move-to>/<drive name>/<its path on the drive> (here /media/archive/Unsorted/old-drive/Photos/2016/… ), read back to check the copy, and only then deleted from the old drive. The place to move to can't be inside what's being freed. Names are kept as they are: if a different file is already there under a name the destination takes for the same one, the file is left in place. On a Mac or Windows, a file whose extended attributes or alternate data streams couldn't be kept on the copy is left in place too, and the message says what couldn't be kept. For a tidier result, file the drive into your archive first; afterwards everything on it has a copy.

Add --go , and type the drive names the dry run showed after --confirm : backdown wipe /media/old-drive --move-to /media/archive/Unsorted --go --confirm "old-drive" Copy For every file, in turn: It must still be what the index says: same size and modification time. A file that changed, or is new since the last scan, is left alone. It's read again and hashed. If it no longer matches its hash, it's left alone. A copy outside the selection is found in the index and read again too. Only if it's there and identical is the file deleted. On Windows, the copy must also have the same alternate data streams. A copy that's only on another machine is used when there's none here: that machine reads it again, in full, just before the deletion. With no copy: with --move-to , it's moved (copied, verified, deleted); without, it's left. The deletion is written to BackDown's journal with its proof: which copy, its hash, and how it was checked. Folders the wipe leaves empty are removed; the drive's own top folder stays. Files that couldn't be read at the last scan are left in place, and so are online-only cloud files on Windows, which would have to be downloaded to be read. --trust-index skips the two reads: it checks that the copy is still there with the size and modification time it had when it was scanned, and trusts the hashes in the index (a copy on another machine is checked the same way, there). It's much faster and, right after a fresh scan and hash of both drives, nearly as safe, but a file that quietly went bad since its last hash wouldn't be noticed. Note A drive mounted read-only can't be wiped; the message says so. Remount it read-write first.

When the background service runs the wipe, it rescans the drives involved afterwards. Without it, index the drive again. If the wipe removed everything, the drive is now empty, and indexing an empty drive needs --allow-empty : backdown index /media/old-drive --allow-empty Copy

backdown wipe stops before doing anything if what you named is: part of the running operating system: / , /usr , /etc , /var , /boot , /System , /Applications and the like, or anything else on the file system the computer runs from, outside the home folders; a whole home folder, such as /home/you or C:\Users\you (folders inside it are fine); on Windows, the system drive itself or Windows , Program Files or ProgramData on it; BackDown's own index, or the folder holding it; not on an indexed drive. Other drives are fine wherever they're mounted: /media , /mnt , /run/media , other drive letters. The machine-wide service never wipes; run backdown --local wipe … from your own account.

The Free up view does the same, with the background service doing the work: Tick drives, folders, files or recognised things under "What to wipe". Each drive shows how much of it exists elsewhere; right-click anything in the browser and choose "Free up" to start from there. "What would happen" shows, for each, how much has an identical copy and where, how much exists only there, and anything that can't be wiped, and why. Under "What exists only here", choose "Move it first, to" a folder, or "Leave it where it is". The view shows the free space there. Under "Before deleting", "Trust the index" is the same as --trust-index . Type the drive names to confirm, and press Wipe . The wipe shows in Activity, and the view lists past wipes with what existed only there and what happened to it. When some copies are only on another machine, "What would happen" says how much, and when that machine last confirmed them. The browser opened with backdown serve shows what would happen but can't wipe: that needs the background service.

Let BackDown propose where everything on your old drives goes in one archive, and why, then copy it there with every file verified. Nothing is deleted. You have several old drives and want everything on them in one archive, sorted into something sensible, with nothing lost and nothing copied twice. BackDown does it in two steps: a plan that says where each thing goes and why, which you can read and change, then apply , which copies, reads every copy back to check it, and keeps a journal. Neither step deletes anything. Once the archive is indexed, the old drives can be freed up . Afterwards, identical files inside the archive can share their storage ( tidy the archive ). The filing plan is marked Pro; in this beta everything is unlocked ( Free and Pro ).
File your old drives into one archive

Index the old drives and the drive the archive will live on, so BackDown knows what's already there: backdown index /media/old-drive /media/laptop-2012 /media/archive backdown hash Copy The plan is built from what BackDown recognises : mail stores, phone backups, Time Machine sets, home folders, photo libraries and so on, with where they came from. plan recognises any drive that needs it, with the drives connected so it can read their backup scripts and plists; backdown entities shows you what it found beforehand, and the daemon keeps it up to date after every scan.
File your old drives into one archive

Name the archive folder, on the drive that will keep everything: backdown plan --to /media/archive/Archive Copy Plan 1: file 1 drive into /media/archive/Archive Copy 60 MB Disk image: VDI image (old-drive) /media/old-drive/VM/win10.vdi → /media/archive/Archive/DiskImages/old-drive/win10.vdi Disk image → DiskImages; newest file 2020 119 MB Folder (old-drive) /media/old-drive/Photos → /media/archive/Archive/Unsorted/old-drive/Photos not recognised as anything in particular: kept as it is, under its drive's name Drives old-drive 182 MB: copy 182 MB, already archived 0 B; every file will have a copy In all: 182 MB in 44 files. Next: `backdown apply 1` shows exactly what would happen; `backdown apply 1 --go` does it. Copy Every indexed drive except the archive's own is filed, unless you name some with --from (repeat it for several). Each item says what it is, where it goes, and why. The plan is saved; backdown plans lists the ones you've made. How things are placed Each kind of thing has a place in the archive, by type, then origin, then time. A mail store from mail.example.org goes to Mail/mail.example.org , an iPhone backup to Phones/<device>/<year> , a git repository to Code/<origin>/<name> . The origin comes from what BackDown found out about it (the server a backup script copied from, the phone's name, the computer's host name, a repository's remote); without one, it's the drive's name. Folders that aren't recognised as anything in particular keep their shape under Unsorted/<drive>/ , and loose files at a drive's top level go to Unsorted/<drive>/(top level) . A few rules keep the archive free of repeats: Already archived. Something whose bytes are already at least 99.9% inside the archive folder isn't copied: "already in the archive at …". Near twins. When two things of the same kind and origin are at least 90% identical (the same mailbox on two old drives, say), only what's unique to the second one is copied, into Also from <drive>/<name> inside the first one's folder. If it's all in the first, it isn't copied at all. Two copies of a mailbox (Maildir or a mail store) can instead be merged by Message-ID into one: --merge-mail , or Merge these mailboxes in the Plan view. Low-value piles. Downloads folders and recovered-file dumps ( found.000 , recup_dir , lost+found ) are listed, not copied. Caches (caches, thumbnails, build output, trash) are copied by default, because a drive can only be proven safe to wipe when every file has a copy. The browser's "Leave out caches, previews and build output" box, or skip_junk = true in a schema, leaves them out; they then stay behind when you free up the drive. Your own schema The places are a small TOML file you can change: backdown plan --print-schema > schema.toml backdown plan --to /media/archive/Archive --schema schema.toml Copy [place] mail-store = "Mail/{origin}" ios-backup = "Phones/{origin}/{year}" photos = "Media/Photos/{name} ({drive})" unsorted = "Unsorted/{drive}/{name}" # … one line for every kind [options] # downloads piles and recovered fragments: list them, but don't copy skip_low_value = true # regenerable caches, previews, build output and trash: copy them too skip_junk = false # a thing at least this identical to another of its kind and origin copies only its own files merge_overlap = 0.9 Copy Places are relative paths inside the archive, and can use {origin} , {name} , {title} , {drive} , {year} and {years} . Characters that don't belong in file names become - .

backdown apply 1 Copy Dry run of plan 1: 44 files (182 MB) to copy into /media/archive/Archive. Nothing was written. Run `backdown apply 1 --go` to copy. Copy The dry run reads the drives and writes nothing. It needs every source drive connected, says what's already done from an earlier run, what's already in the archive, and which destinations already exist, and checks the archive's drive has room.

backdown apply 1 --go Copy Each file is copied under a temporary name beside its destination ( .<name>.backdown-partial ), hashed as it's written, flushed to disk, given the original's modification time, renamed into place, then read back and compared. A copy that reads back differently is removed and reported. Where the archive's drive allows it, copies are made faster: as clones that share the original's blocks (btrfs, XFS, APFS, when the old drive is the same file system) or by the kernel (Linux); they're read back all the same. Along the way: an existing file at the destination is never overwritten: if it's identical it counts as already there, and if it differs it's left alone and reported as a conflict; a name the archive's drive would take for another one ( Photo.jpg beside photo.jpg on a Mac or Windows drive), or can't hold at all, is copied under another name ( photo (2).jpg ), and the journal says so ( copies across file systems ); on a Mac, extended attributes are copied too, and on Windows alternate data streams; what couldn't be kept is listed; nothing is ever deleted from the old drives; symbolic links aren't copied (the summary counts them); every file is written to a journal, so an interrupted run carries on where it stopped when you run the same command again. It ends with a summary (how many were cloned or copied by the kernel, renamed, or kept without some attributes), and exits with 2 when there were conflicts or failures to look at. When the background service is running, --go is handed to it (you follow the progress in the terminal), and it indexes the archive afterwards.

Copies only count as proof once the archive is indexed. Without the daemon: backdown index /media/archive backdown check /media/old-drive Copy When check says SAFE TO WIPE , the old drive can be freed up .

An archive filled from several old drives still holds identical files in different places: the same photo filed under two albums, a backup inside a backup. backdown dedup makes identical files inside one folder share their storage, without taking any of them away: backdown dedup /media/archive/Archive Copy /media/archive/Archive (ext4): hardlinks 412 sets of identical files: 530 files would be linked, saving 38.2 GB 17 identical files kept apart: their permissions, owner or extended attributes, or modification time, differ from every other copy's Biggest savings: 4.7 GB Backups/laptop-2019/VM/win10.vdi ← DiskImages/old-drive/win10.vdi Hardlinked files are one file with several names: editing any of them changes them all. To make one a separate file again, copy it and replace it with the copy (cp -p photo.jpg photo.tmp && mv photo.tmp photo.jpg). Nothing was changed. To link them: backdown dedup "/media/archive/Archive" --link hard --go Copy There are two ways to share: Hardlinks ( --link hard , the default) work on any drive that has them: the files become one file with several names, so editing one edits them all. For an archive you only add to, that's usually what you want. Clones ( --link clone ) work on btrfs, XFS and APFS: they stay separate files that share their blocks until one of them changes. It only links files the index says are identical (index and hash the folder first), on the same drive, inside the folder you name; files smaller than 4 KB are left alone ( --min-size ). Files whose permissions, owner or extended attributes differ (and, for hardlinks, their modification time) are kept apart, and so are files that also have names outside the folder. Without --go it only shows what it would do. With --go , each pair is read again first and must still match the index's hash; the link is made under a temporary name and swapped in only if nothing changed meanwhile; and every link is journaled in the index. An interrupted run carries on when you run it again. Index the drive afterwards so BackDown sees the links (the background service does it for you). It exits with 2 if any file failed. It refuses the running system, whole home folders and BackDown's own index, like freeing up does. It isn't available on Windows yet, where linking could lose files' alternate data streams.

The Plan view does the same: With no plan yet, "New plan" asks for the archive folder (each drive's /Archive is suggested), which drives to file, and whether to leave out caches. Press Make plan . The plan shows each drive (to copy, already archived, and what would stay only there), then the items under "Copy", "Copy only what's unique" and "Not copied", each with its source, destination and why. Merge these mailboxes , on an item that has a twin, merges the two by Message-ID instead of copying one's extra files beside the other. Dry run reports what applying would do. Apply asks you to confirm, then copies in the background service; follow it in Activity. Making a plan works in the browser opened with backdown serve ; applying needs the background service. At the bottom of the Plan view, Tidy the archive does what backdown dedup does: choose the folder (the plan's archive is suggested), Hardlinks or Clones , and the smallest size, then See what it would save , and Link to start it in the background service.
