Turn copies of the same mailbox taken at different times into one Maildir, every message once and in the right folder, and export a folder as mbox. The copies are only read. Old drives often hold the same mailbox several times: a laptop's mail from 2016, a server backup from 2019, Thunderbird's local folders from last year. Each has most of the same messages, and each has a few the others don't. BackDown merges them into one Maildir with every message once, by Message-ID, in the folder the newest copy has it in, with the read, replied and flagged marks of all of them. The copies are only read.

Maildir , including Maildir++ subfolders ( .Sent , .Archives.2019 ) and Dovecot's folder-per-folder layout; mbox files , one per folder; a Thunderbird account folder ( Mail/Local Folders or ImapMail/<server> in a profile): its mbox files and their .sbd subfolders; whole mail stores , folders of Maildirs such as a mail server's domain/user/Maildir , merged mailbox by mailbox. Give either mailboxes or stores, not a mix. Dovecot's mdbox and sdbox formats aren't read yet.
See what the merge would be

backdown mail merge /media/old-drive/Mail/ann /media/laptop-2012/Thunderbird/Mail/Local\ Folders /media/archive/Backups/mail-2021/ann/Maildir \ --to /media/archive/Archive/Mail/ann --dry-run Copy Snapshots, oldest first: 1. /media/old-drive/Mail/ann (Maildir): 6.2 K messages, the newest from 1 Jun 2019 only in this one: 212 messages folders only here: Old 2. /media/laptop-2012/Thunderbird/Mail/Local Folders (mbox folder): 5.9 K messages, the newest from 3 Mar 2020 3. /media/archive/Backups/mail-2021/ann/Maildir (Maildir): 6.8 K messages, the newest from 9 Feb 2021 folders only here: Archive Would merge 7.3 K distinct messages (1.4 GB), in 4 folders; 11.6 K duplicate copies left out without a Message-ID (matched by headers and body): 38 in another folder in an older snapshot (placed where the newest has them): 144 copies differing only in headers a server or mail program added (the newest kept): 902 flags combined from several copies (read, replied or flagged in any): 1.1 K Folders: Archive 1.2 K · INBOX 5.6 K · Old 212 · Sent 310 Nothing was written. Without --dry-run, the merged mailbox goes to /media/archive/Archive/Mail/ann Copy The dry run reads every message and writes nothing. The copies are ordered by their newest message, whatever order you name them in.
How messages are matched and placed

Two copies are the same message when they have the same Message-ID and the same body. The same Message-ID with a different body is kept twice. A message without a Message-ID is matched by its headers and body, leaving out headers that servers and mail programs add or change (status, UIDs, keywords and the like). Each message goes in the folder the newest copy that has it keeps it in, so messages you filed later end up filed. One that was deleted since stays in the folder it was in. If the newest copy has it in two folders, it's in both. The message written is the newest copy's, exactly as stored (from an mbox, without its From line and quoting). Read, replied, flagged and forwarded marks are combined from every copy; draft and trashed come from the copy that's kept. In a mail store, messages are matched mailbox by mailbox: the same message in two people's mailboxes stays in both.

backdown mail merge /media/old-drive/Mail/ann /media/laptop-2012/Thunderbird/Mail/Local\ Folders /media/archive/Backups/mail-2021/ann/Maildir \ --to /media/archive/Archive/Mail/ann Copy The destination must be a new or empty folder (or one this merge already started). It becomes a Maildir++ mailbox: the inbox is the folder itself, and other folders are .Name inside it ( .Archives.2019 for nested ones), the layout Dovecot and Courier use, and most mail servers and programs that read Maildir understand. Each message is written under a temporary name, flushed to disk, moved into place, then read back and compared, and journaled in BackDown's index. An interrupted merge carries on where it stopped when you run the same command again. It ends with "Written and verified", and exits with 2 if any message couldn't be read or written. With the background service running, the merge is handed to it (it shows in Activity as "Merge mailboxes"), and the destination's drive is indexed afterwards.

A filing plan notices mailboxes of the same origin that are at least 90% the same (the same Maildir or mail store on two old drives, say). By default it files one and copies only the other's extra files beside it, into Also from <drive>/… . To merge them instead: backdown plan --to /media/archive/Archive --merge-mail merges every such pair; in the Plan view, Merge these mailboxes on an item does it for that one, before the plan is applied. Applying the plan then writes one merged mailbox for each ("Merge snapshots of a mailbox (by Message-ID)" in the plan), store by store and mailbox by mailbox. The plan's dry run doesn't read the messages; backdown mail merge … --dry-run on the same folders shows what the merge will be.

backdown mail export /media/archive/Archive/Mail/ann/.Sent --mbox /media/archive/Exports/ann-sent.mbox Copy exported 310 messages (48 MB) to /media/archive/Exports/ann-sent.mbox as mboxrd, read back and verified Only this folder's messages (not its subfolders); read, replied and flagged marks aren't kept: mbox has no standard place for them. Copy It writes one Maildir folder's own messages, oldest first, as an mbox file (the mboxrd kind, which quotes From lines so they come back exactly). The file must not exist yet, and can't be inside the Maildir. It's written under a temporary name and read back before it takes its name. backdown mail is free; merging in a plan is part of the filing plan, which is marked Pro ( Free and Pro ).

Keep a folder, usually part of your archive, copied on another drive, with changed files' old copies kept aside and a sample re-read now and then. An archive on one drive is one failure away from gone. A mirror keeps a second copy of a folder on another drive and checks it: new and changed files are copied and verified, nothing on the mirror is ever deleted, and a different sample of the mirror is read back regularly to catch copies that went bad.

backdown mirror add /media/archive/Archive/Mail /media/backup/Mail Copy Mirror 1: /media/archive/Archive/Mail → /media/backup/Mail Copy it now with `backdown mirror sync 1`; the BackDown service syncs daily and re-reads a sample every 30 days. Copy The first folder must exist; the mirror folder is created on the first sync. Neither may be inside the other. --verify-every 7 re-reads a sample every 7 days instead of 30.

backdown mirror sync Copy mirror 1: 1 copied (3 MB), 1 updated (old copies kept in .backdown-versions), 30 unchanged, 1 only on the mirror (kept) Copy Without a number, every mirror is synced. A file with the same size and modification time on both sides is unchanged. New files are copied and read back to check them, as clones or by the kernel where the drives allow it, like copies into an archive . A name the mirror's drive would take for another one, or can't hold, is copied under another name, and extended attributes (Mac) and alternate data streams (Windows) go along; mirror sync lists what it renamed or couldn't keep. When a file changed, the mirror's old copy is first moved to .backdown-versions/<time>/ inside the mirror folder, so an accidental change on the original never destroys the only good copy. A sync never deletes. Files that exist only on the mirror (because they were deleted from the original, say) are kept and counted. Symbolic links aren't copied. Check the mirror drive has room: sync doesn't check free space first.

backdown mirror verify backdown mirror verify 1 --all Copy mirror 1: re-read 31 files (99 MB): all identical Copy By default a 5% sample is read back ( --percent 10 for more), and it's a different 5% each day, so repeated checks cover the whole mirror over time. --all reads every file. Each is compared with the original's hash in the index when that's current, or with the original itself. Missing files, different sizes or contents, and unreadable files are listed, and the command exits with 2.

With the background service running, you don't need to run these by hand. Whenever both drives are connected, it syncs each mirror once a day and re-reads a 5% sample when a verify is due. The browser's Activity view lists the mirrors, whether both drives are there, and when each was last synced and verified. A verify that finds differences becomes a notification, and when a mirror's drive reports a warning or that it's failing ( drive health ), Activity says "This mirror drive is dying" and suggests a second mirror on a healthy drive. backdown mirror list Copy 1 /media/archive/Archive/Mail → /media/backup/Mail synced 2026-09-28 23:30 UTC: 31 files: 1 copied (3 MB), 1 updated (old copies kept), 30 unchanged, 1 only on the mirror verified 2026-09-28 23:30 UTC: re-read 31 files (99 MB, 100%): all identical Copy To stop keeping a mirror, backdown mirror remove 1 . The copies stay where they are.

Let copies on a NAS or another computer count, reached over ssh with your own keys: add a machine, sync it, browse it, and free up drives here against copies there. Your archive may be on a NAS, and old drives plugged into a different computer. BackDown on this computer can read another machine's BackDown index over ssh, so files there count as copies: for duplicates, for overlaps, for check , and for freeing up drives here. Nothing on the other machine is ever changed, and no file's contents are sent: only its index entries and, when asked, SHA-256 hashes. Several machines is marked Pro ; in this beta everything is unlocked ( Free and Pro ).

On the other machine (Linux or macOS): Install BackDown, and index its drives there ( backdown index , or its own background service). BackDown here reads that index; it doesn't index the other machine's drives itself. Make sure you can log in to it with ssh without a password, with a key: ssh-copy-id you@nas.example.org sets that up. Connect once with ssh in a terminal, to check and accept its host key. BackDown never asks for a password and never accepts an unknown host key on your behalf, so these have to work first.

backdown remote add nas ssh://you@nas.example.org Copy Added nas (ssh://you@nas.example.org). Reached nas (nas): BackDown 1.0.0-beta.1, index /var/lib/backdown/index.db, 2 drives indexed: /volume1, /volume2 Next: backdown remote sync nas (the BackDown service also syncs it every 6 h) Copy The name is yours (like nas or office-pc ). The address is ssh://[user@]host[:port] , or a host alias from your ~/.ssh/config . BackDown there finds its index the way it would itself (its own service's, or its default); if it's elsewhere, --remote-db /path/to/index.db . If backdown isn't on the PATH an ssh session gets there, --backdown /usr/local/bin/backdown . backdown remote test nas tries the connection again at any time. In the app, the sidebar's Machines section has Add a machine , with the same fields.

backdown remote sync Copy nas: 2 drives, 412.8 K files (412.8 K new or changed, 0 gone); 1.2 K sampled and 310 hashed there for comparison Copy A sync fetches what changed in the other machine's index since the last one, by that machine's scans. Then, so that copies can be proved, files there whose size matches a file here are sampled there, and those whose samples match are hashed there in full; after the sync, BackDown hashes files here against what's there. The other machine reads only what it has to, and each sync spends at most 20 minutes hashing there; what's left waits for the next one. With the background service running, you don't need to: it syncs each machine every 6 hours ( backdown remote settings --sync-hours 12 changes that), one at a time, beside its other work, and hashes here afterwards. A scheduled sync that fails becomes a notification. Syncing runs in your own BackDown: the machine-wide service has no ssh keys of yours. backdown remote list Copy nas ssh://you@nas.example.org (index /var/lib/backdown/index.db) synced 2 h ago /volume1 398.1 K files, 1.80 TB · scanned there 2 days ago · its copies count /volume2 14.7 K files, 96.0 GB · scanned there 9 days ago · too long ago for its copies to count Copies on another machine count when confirmed there within 7 days (backdown remote settings --proof-days N). Copy

A file on another machine counts as a copy of a file here only when: both have the same SHA-256 and size (never by name or size alone); it could be read there, and hasn't changed since that machine's scan; it was confirmed there recently: that machine's last scan of its drive, as synced here, finished within the last 7 days, or that machine read the file again for BackDown within them. backdown remote settings --proof-days 14 changes the window (1 to 90 days). So the other machine has to keep being scanned (its own background service does it), and synced. A copy that's too old says so: "more than 7 days ago, so it doesn't count until nas has been scanned and synced again". Where they show: backdown check says how much of what's verified is only on another machine: "of the verified, 1.2 GB in 3 files are only on another machine (nas (ssh://you@nas.example.org)): hashed there and confirmed there within 7 days". A drive can be safe to wipe with some of its copies there. The browser's Duplicates view lists copies there ("on nas : /volume1/Photos/…"), and "Here once, and again on another machine" for files with one copy here and one there. backdown dupes in a terminal lists only this computer's. A file's details list "On other machines", each with when it was confirmed and whether it counts. backdown overlaps counts a machine as a place copies can be ("on nas").
Free up a drive against copies there

Freeing up uses a copy on another machine only when there's no copy on this one. The dry run says how much that is. Then, just before deleting such a file here, BackDown has the other machine read its copy again, in full, and compares the SHA-256 with the file here, which has just been read again too. Only if they match is the file deleted, and the journal records the copy there ( ssh://…/path , "remote re-read") as its proof. If the machine can't be reached, or its copy changed, the file stays here (or, with --move-to , is moved first). With --trust-index , the other machine only checks that its copy is still there as it last scanned it, and answers with the hash in its index, without reading the file.

Each machine in the sidebar opens its page: whether it can be reached, when it was synced, its drives (and whether their copies count), Sync now , Test connection and Remove… . Its drives can be browsed, read-only: live over ssh as its last scan saw them, or from what was synced when it can't be reached. A file's details show its hash there and its copies here and elsewhere. Files there don't open or preview here: "To open it, open it on nas: BackDown doesn't bring files over from other machines." To forget a machine: backdown remote remove nas (or Remove… ). Nothing on it is touched; its copies stop counting here.

BackDown runs your system's own ssh , as you, with your keys, agent, known_hosts and ~/.ssh/config . It adds BatchMode=yes , so ssh never asks for a password, and turns off agent and X11 forwarding. Host keys are checked as your ssh configuration says. Nothing listens on the network, here or there. On the other machine, ssh starts backdown serve-stdio , which answers questions about its index over the ssh connection and exits when it closes. It opens the index read-only, never creates or changes one, and reads a file only to hash it when asked, and only if it's still as indexed. What travels is index entries (paths, sizes, dates, hashes) and hashes, never files' contents.

It says What to do "ssh couldn't log in to nas with your keys" Add your public key there ( ssh-copy-id ), or load it into your ssh agent "nas's host key isn't known here, or it changed" Connect once with ssh in a terminal, check the key and accept it "backdown isn't installed on nas, or isn't on the PATH ssh sessions get there" Add the machine with --backdown /full/path/to/backdown "there's no BackDown index at … on nas" Index something there first, or give its index with --remote-db "the BackDown on nas is too old to be reached this way", or a protocol mismatch Update the older one "nas didn't answer" Is it on, and on this network?
Windows computers can't be the other end yet (they can be this end). Files on another machine can't be opened or previewed here, and drive health isn't shared between machines.

What each drive says about itself, what BackDown can read of it on Linux, macOS and Windows, the warnings and trends it keeps, notifications, and what to do when a drive is failing. Drives keep a record of how they're doing: sectors they've had to replace, sectors they can't read, errors on the cable, how much of an SSD's write endurance is used, temperature, and their own overall verdict (SMART). BackDown reads it for every physical drive, keeps a history of it, and tells you when a drive gets worse, so that you copy what's on it while it still reads. It only reads. It never runs the drive's own self-tests, and never changes a setting on it.

In the app, Activity's "Connected drives" has a pill beside each disk ( healthy , warning , failing or no health data ), and the sidebar marks an indexed drive with a warning or failing dot. Click a pill for the details. In a terminal: backdown health Copy DRIVE MODEL SERIAL HEALTH TEMP HOURS REALLOC PEND UNC CRC WEAR SINCE FIRST READING sdc WDC WD5000AAKX-00ERMA0 WD-WCC000000000 warning 36°C 20.0 K 6 2 0 0 - 29 Sep 2026: +6 reallocated, +2 pending nvme0n1 Samsung SSD 970 EVO 1TB S000NX0000000000 ok 35°C 4.1 K - - - - 3% first reading sdc: 6 sectors had gone bad and have been replaced by spares (reallocated) sdc: 2 sectors can't be read and are waiting to be replaced (pending) Copy The columns are the temperature, hours powered on, reallocated, pending and uncorrectable sectors, cable (CRC) errors, and wear, then what changed since BackDown first read the drive. Lines after the table explain each finding, and any note: says what couldn't be read and how to read more. --json gives everything, history included. backdown health exits with 2 when a connected drive is failing, so a script can watch for it. With the background service running (on Linux and macOS), it asks the service to read every drive now; otherwise it reads them itself.

Everything is read as you, without administrator rights. What an ordinary account is told depends on the system: System How What it gets Linux udisks, over the system bus Most SATA drives' verdict, temperature, hours and bad-sector counts, and NVMe drives' health (with udisks 2.10 or later). With busctl installed, reallocated and pending sectors separately; without it, together Linux smartctl , if it's installed and your account may open the drive (usually only root or the disk group) Everything the drive reports, on top of udisks Linux sysfs A temperature, where nothing else gave one macOS diskutil The drive's verdict and, for NVMe drives on recent macOS, wear, spare blocks, media errors, temperature and hours macOS smartctl , if installed ( brew install smartmontools ) More drives, NVMe fully, USB where the enclosure passes it on Windows the storage cmdlets Every drive's overall health, to everyone; its temperature, wear and error counters only to an administrator What it can't read, it says, with the command that would, for example: "needs administrator rights: sudo smartctl -a /dev/sdc"; "its USB enclosure doesn't pass health data on", which is common: many USB cases and docks don't; on Windows, "Windows shares this drive's error counters only with an administrator": running backdown health once in an administrator terminal reads them. smartctl is asked not to wake a drive that has spun down; a sleeping drive keeps its last reading until it's awake. udisks answers from what it already knows.

A drive is failing when it says so itself, when it marks an attribute as failing now, when an NVMe drive's spare blocks fall below its own limit or it reports media errors that degrade it, or when bad sectors pile up (100 or more reallocated, or 10 or more pending or uncorrectable). It's a warning for any reallocated, pending or uncorrectable sector, unrecoverable media errors, spare blocks running low, 90% or more of an SSD's rated write endurance used, or running hot (55 °C for a spinning disk, 70 °C for others). Cable errors alone don't change the verdict: they usually mean a cable or an enclosure, not the drive. Unknown means there's no health data at all.

Each reading is kept in the index under the drive's serial number, so its history follows it from one port or enclosure to another: whenever something changed, and at least once every 20 hours otherwise. The details show the counters, small charts of temperature, bad sectors, wear, cable and media errors since the first reading, what changed since then ("+6 reallocated"), and a list of what changed and when. The background service reads every connected drive 20 seconds after it starts, then every six hours, when a disk is plugged in (on Linux and macOS), when an indexed drive comes back, and when you press Check now .

When a reading is worse than the one before, the service tells you, in Activity's Notifications and, unless you've turned them off, on your desktop: Notice When " drive is failing" its verdict became failing " drive needs watching" its verdict became warning " drive is getting worse" with the verdict unchanged: more bad sectors or media errors, wear crossed 80, 90 or 100%, or it ran hot (it reached the hot mark, 10 °C or more above the last reading) "Transfer errors on drive " only its cable errors rose: "check or replace the cable or enclosure; the drive itself may be fine" A failing drive's notice always reaches the desktop, however many others were shown. If a mirror's copy is on that drive, the notice says so: "this mirror drive is dying, add another mirror". Notifications has the settings and the limits.

A connected drive that's failing gets a banner across the app: what's wrong, and Copy it now . It opens Rescue with that drive chosen and "It's failing" selected, so the next step is choosing where the copy goes (another drive: it suggests BackDown Rescue/<drive> <date>.img on one of your indexed drives) and pressing Start copying . A failing drive can stop reading at any moment, and every read wears it further: copy it once, the good areas first, then look for files in the copy rather than on the drive. If the drive only needs watching, make sure what's on it has a copy elsewhere: backdown check on it says whether it does ( what "safe to wipe" means ).
BackDown doesn't start SMART self-tests or read their logs, and doesn't share health readings with other machines : each machine's BackDown reads its own drives.

Copy a failing drive or memory card safely, find deleted photos and documents by their contents, and look for lost partitions and the files on them. BackDown only reads the drive. Three things can go wrong with a drive or a memory card, and Rescue has an answer for each: What happened What to do Command It's failing: clicks, freezes, read errors, very slow Copy it into an image first, the good areas before the bad backdown rescue image Files were deleted, or it was formatted Find photos, videos and documents by what's inside them backdown rescue find It looks empty, or a partition vanished Look for file systems the partition table no longer lists, and browse them backdown rescue partitions Deleted files can often come back with their names too, from FAT, exFAT and NTFS: Recover deleted files . Rescue only ever reads the drive. Whatever it saves goes to another drive: it refuses to write the image or the files it finds onto the drive being rescued. Careful If a drive is failing, every read counts. Copy it into an image first, then look for files and partitions in the image, not on the drive. BackDown can tell you a drive is failing before it stops: backdown health and the browser show what each drive reports about itself ( drive health ), and a failing drive gets a banner with Copy it now , which opens Rescue set up to copy it.

In the browser, the Rescue view lists every disk and partition. In a terminal, backdown volumes does, with model, size, serial number and file systems; or use lsblk on Linux and diskutil list on macOS. Drives are device files such as /dev/sdc on Linux or /dev/disk4 on macOS. Every rescue command also takes an image file instead of a drive.
When BackDown can't read the drive

Reading a whole drive directly needs a permission your account usually doesn't have. BackDown says so, and gives the one command that lets your account read that one drive, and never change it, until it's unplugged or the computer restarts: backdown: can't read /dev/sdc: reading a whole drive directly needs permission your user account doesn't have Run it as an administrator (sudo backdown rescue image …), or let your account read that drive: sudo setfacl -m u:you:r /dev/sdc Copy On macOS the command is sudo chmod o+r /dev/disk4 . On Windows, run the terminal as administrator. Running Rescue itself with sudo is fine too: it never opens BackDown's index, and what it writes is handed back to you rather than left owned by root. Allow BackDown to read this drive On Linux, the Rescue view has a third way: Allow BackDown to read this drive . BackDown asks udisks, the system's disk service, to open the drive for it read-only, and the system shows its own password dialog. Nothing of BackDown's runs as root, and the drive can't be changed through what it's given. It lasts until the background service stops; if the dialog is closed or the system refuses, the terminal command above still works. If the drive is in use (mounted, say), udisks may refuse to open it this way.
Copy a failing drive into an image

backdown rescue image /dev/sdc /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img Copy Copying /dev/sdc (500.1 GB) into /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img The map: /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img.map Ctrl+C stops it; run the same command again to carry on. Copy It works the way GNU ddrescue does. The first passes copy what reads easily, forwards and then backwards, skipping ahead past slow or bad areas instead of hammering at them. Later passes go back to the edges of the bad areas, then read what's left sector by sector, and finally retry unreadable sectors ( --retries 3 for more tries). Unreadable parts stay as zeros in the image. A map beside the image records what's been read, in GNU ddrescue's own format. It's saved every few seconds, so you can stop the copy at any time, or lose power, and run the same command to carry on where it left off. When it's done: Copied 500.1 GB of 500.1 GB; 12 KB couldn't be read, in 3 places. Running it again with --retries 3 tries those again. Copy It exits with 0 when everything was read, and 2 when some of it couldn't be. It won't start if: the image would be on the drive being rescued, or on another partition of the same physical drive ( --same-drive allows that for a drive that isn't failing); the destination doesn't have room for what's left to copy, or is formatted FAT32, which can't hold a file of 4 GB or more (it says so); an image of that name exists without its map (it's never overwritten).

backdown rescue find /media/archive/Rescue/sdc.img --to /media/archive/Rescue/sdc-files Copy This looks through every byte for the signatures of files, whatever the file system says: after files were deleted, the card was formatted, or the file system is damaged. What it recognises: Kind Types Photos JPEG, HEIC, PNG, GIF, WebP, BMP, AVIF, TIFF, camera RAW (CR2, CR3, NEF, ARW, DNG, ORF, RW2, PEF, SRW, RAF) Videos MP4, MOV, M4V, 3GP, AVI, MKV, WebM, WMV, MTS, TS, MPEG, OGV Audio MP3, M4A, WAV, FLAC, Ogg, Opus, AIFF, WMA Documents PDF, Word, Excel and PowerPoint (old and new), OpenDocument, EPUB, Outlook messages Archives ZIP, RAR, 7z Other SQLite databases, other Office-format files --only photos,documents narrows it to groups or types ( --only jpg,pdf ). What's found is saved in a folder per kind, named after where it was found on the drive, with the list in found.jsonl : Found 1.3 K files (6.1 GB): 1.2 K photos, 40 videos, 12 documents In /media/archive/Rescue/sdc-files (the list: /media/archive/Rescue/sdc-files/found.jsonl) Copy Files found this way have no names, folders or dates of their own (photos and videos keep the dates inside them). A file that was stored in scattered pieces comes back damaged, or not at all: finding by content can't put pieces back together. A file whose end isn't found is kept up to a size limit for its type and counted as cut off. When the daemon does the finding, it indexes what it found, so the files open in the browser.

backdown rescue partitions /dev/sdc Copy It reads the partition table (MBR, including logical partitions, or GPT, checking both of its copies), then looks for file systems where partitions usually start, and at every sector with --deep (as slow as copying the drive). File systems are found by their own structures, including their backups when the start is damaged: NTFS, exFAT, FAT, ext2/3/4, XFS, btrfs, APFS, HFS+, F2FS, SquashFS, ReFS, ISO 9660 and UDF; encrypted LUKS and BitLocker volumes, LVM, RAID members and swap are recognised as such. /dev/sdc (500.1 GB): no partition table Starts at byte Sector Size File system Name In the table 1048576 2048 500.1 GB NTFS Photos NO: lost 1 not in the table. To get files out of one: backdown rescue find /dev/sdc --to <folder> --start <byte> --end <byte> Copy It never changes the partition table. To get files out of a lost partition: In the browser, a FAT, exFAT, ext or NTFS file system that was found gets Browse files : its folders and files as they are, read-only, with its deleted files if you ask, and copying out to another drive ( Recover deleted files ). For any file system, "Find files in it" in the browser, or rescue find on just that range (its start, and its start plus its size), finds files by their contents.

The Rescue view asks three questions: Which drive or card? Every disk and partition, or an image file. It checks BackDown can read it and, if it can't, shows the permission command with a Copy button and "Check again" (and, on Linux, Allow BackDown to read this drive ). What happened? "It's failing", "Files were deleted, or it was formatted", or "It looks empty, or a partition vanished". Where should it go? A folder on another drive (it suggests BackDown Rescue/<drive> <date> on one of your indexed drives), and what to look for. Rescues run in the background service beside scans and hashing, show their progress (a copy shows a map of what's been read), can be stopped and resumed, and stay on the list afterwards. From a finished copy you can go straight to "Find files in the copy" or "Look for partitions in the copy", and from a partition that was found to "Browse files" or "Find files in it". Rescues need the background service; the machine-wide service doesn't do them, so run backdown rescue from your own account. A copy that's an image file on an indexed drive also opens in the browser, where the files on its FAT, exFAT, ext and NTFS partitions can be browsed; for other file systems (XFS, btrfs, HFS+, APFS), the image can be mounted read-only by the system instead ( disk images ).

Finding files by content can't put a file stored in scattered pieces back together. Partitions Rescue finds with file systems BackDown doesn't read itself (XFS, btrfs, HFS+, APFS and others) can only be searched by content, not browsed or mounted. Browsing, undeleting and copying out are in the browser only, not in backdown rescue .

Open a drive's or card's file system directly, see deleted files with their names and how likely each is intact, and copy them out to another drive, checked. FAT, exFAT and NTFS; ext4 by content instead. When a file is deleted, most file systems only mark its entry and its space as free; the bytes stay until something else is written there. BackDown can read a drive's file system itself, without mounting it, list what's deleted with its original name and folder, say how likely each one is to come back whole, and copy what you choose to another drive, checking every copy. It works on FAT (memory cards, USB sticks), exFAT and NTFS. It only reads the drive. Careful Stop using the drive or card first: every file written to it can land on the space a deleted file still occupies. Don't install anything onto it, and don't save what you recover onto it. If it's failing, copy it into an image first and recover from the image. This is done in the app (Rescue needs the background service); there's no terminal command for it yet.

Open Rescue and choose the drive or card (or an image file of one). If BackDown can't read it directly, it shows how to allow that ( when BackDown can't read the drive ). Under "What happened?", choose It looks empty, or a partition vanished , and start it. This lists every file system on the drive, whether the partition table still lists it or not. It only reads, and is quick. Each FAT, exFAT, ext or NTFS file system found gets Browse files . A disk image on an indexed drive (a raw image, or a fixed-size VHD or VDI) works the same way: open it in the browser, and each partition has Browse files .

Browse files opens the file system as it is now, read-only, with its folders, names, sizes and dates. Tick Show deleted files to add what was deleted, greyed, with a label: Label What it means deleted, recoverable Everything it used is still free. It should come back whole, most likely if it was small or stored in one piece partly overwritten Some of its space has been used by other files since, and those parts come back empty: "about 40% of it is still there" overwritten Other files have been saved where it was. It can't be copied can't be read An NTFS file encrypted with Windows' EFS: it needs the Windows account's keys Hover over a deleted file to see why, and how sure BackDown is, as a percentage. For example: "it fitted in one cluster, and no other file has used it since" (95%); "its MFT record still says where its data is, and no other file has used that space since" (95%); "its clusters are all still free; they're taken to follow one another, as most files are written (if it was stored in pieces, parts may come back wrong)" (70%). That last one is the limit of recovering from FAT: once a file is deleted there, the record of where its pieces were is gone, so BackDown assumes they followed one another, which is true of most files. exFAT often keeps that record (then it's followed), and NTFS keeps it in the file's MFT record. On FAT without long names, the first letter of a deleted file's name is lost and shows as _ . A deleted folder opens too; everything in it is deleted. A deleted file whose folder was deleted as well shows at the top level: "Its folder was deleted too, so it's shown here". Recoverable files preview like any other; parts other files have taken show as empty.

Tick the files and folders you want and choose Copy these out… ; with nothing ticked, the button copies the folder you're in ( Copy this folder out… ), or at the top, Copy everything out… : "Save in" suggests BackDown Rescue/<name> <date> on one of your indexed drives; type a full path to put them elsewhere. It must be on another drive: BackDown refuses a folder on the drive being read, because saving there could overwrite the very files being recovered. With the deleted files in chosen folders copies what's deleted inside the folders you picked, too. Start copying. Each file is written, flushed to disk, read back and compared before it counts; a copy that doesn't read back the same is removed. Nothing at the destination is overwritten: a name that's taken becomes name (2).ext . Characters the destination can't hold become _ . Files keep their modification time. Links aren't copied, and neither are files marked overwritten. The copy shows in Rescue and in Activity, can be stopped and carried on, and ends with what was copied and what couldn't be, with Open the copies . The copies are then indexed, so they open in the browser.

Linux's ext3 and ext4 erase where a deleted file's data was, so deleted files can't be brought back by name. Rescue can still find photos, videos and documents on such a drive by their contents: choose Files were deleted, or it was formatted instead ( find deleted files ). Those come back without their names.

The file system itself is damaged beyond reading, or it's one BackDown doesn't read (XFS, btrfs, APFS, HFS+ and others): use find by content . The drive was formatted: formatting usually replaces the file system's records, so the old names are gone. Find by content. An SSD usually discards deleted space soon after (TRIM): what was there can't be recovered by any tool, and BackDown can't tell from the file system that it's gone. A file in thousands of scattered pieces on FAT comes back wrong, even when it says "recoverable".

Open any file on any indexed drive as it was at any scan, read mailboxes as conversations, see SQL dumps as schemas, look inside disk images, and search every drive at once. The file browser shows everything in the index the way a file manager would, with history: every drive, every folder as it was at any scan, and a viewer for most files, without copying anything back first. It only reads.

backdown serve Copy serve prints a private link and opens it: http://127.0.0.1:8787/?t=… . The browser listens on this computer only, answers only that link (the token becomes a cookie for the session), and makes no requests beyond this computer: the viewers are built in. The app's window ( backdown app ) and backdown open show the background service's browser instead, which can also start scans, copies and rescues; they open it with a one-time code, so the private token never appears on a command line. backdown serve --port 8788 runs a second one next to the service's.

Your indexed drives are in the sidebar, with their size and number of files. Folders open with a double click or Enter ; Alt+↑ goes to the parent, Alt+← back. Grid ( Ctrl+1 ) and list ( Ctrl+2 ) views show the folder; the details pane ( Ctrl+I ) shows a file's versions, its copies on other drives, and a preview. There's more: a photo gallery ( Ctrl+3 ) and a size map ( Ctrl+4 ), filters by type, size and date, sorting, hidden files ( Ctrl+H ), tabs, typing a location ( Ctrl+L , where a drive's name stands for its path), right-click menus, and a dot beside each drive for its health . Press ? for every shortcut. From the right-click menu, "Open with system app" opens a file in the program your computer uses for it, and "Show in file manager" shows where it is. BackDown never opens programs or scripts that way. "Download a copy" saves a copy through your web browser, from any drive or any scan whose bytes still exist.

The bar at the bottom of a drive with two scans or more is the time slider : drag it to see the drive as it was at that scan. Files deleted since are struck through, and those that changed later are marked. Back to now returns. A file's old version opens if its bytes still exist: the file itself, unchanged, or an identical copy on any indexed drive ("Read from … (identical copy)"). Otherwise the index still knows its size, dates and hash, and says the bytes are gone. The details pane lists every version of a file, with Diff against the current one for text. Compare… shows what changed in a folder between any two scans: what was added, removed and changed, with a diff for text files. Files count as the same when their SHA-256 hashes match (or, before they're hashed, their size and modification time).

Ctrl+F searches the folder you're in and everything below it; Ctrl+Shift+F searches every indexed drive. It matches file and folder names, not their contents, ignoring case and accents; with several words, a name must contain all of them. Exact names come first, then names that start with what you typed, then the rest, newest first. Tick "Earlier versions" to find files that were there at earlier scans but aren't now; opening one shows its folder as it was when it was last seen. The first 200 matches show, and "Show more" goes up to 2,000.

Files What you see Photos and images The image, with actual size and fit Audio and video Your browser's player PDF Pages, with zoom Word ( .docx ) The document SQLite databases Tables and views with row counts, 200 rows a page, and each table's SQL; opened read-only Text and code With syntax highlighting, up to 8 MB CSV and TSV A table Git repositories The history, last 300 commits with their changes (needs git installed) Two text files A diff, with how similar they are Spreadsheets ( .xlsx , .xls , .ods and more) Sheets as tables, 500 rows a page Slides ( .pptx , .odp ) Titles, text, images and notes Archives ( .zip , .tar.gz and more) What's inside, and each file in it opens too Mailboxes Conversations: see below SQL dumps The schema: see below Disk images The partitions, and the files inside: see below Anything else The first 4 KB, as hex

Mail opens as conversations, threaded by the headers that link replies together. BackDown reads .mbox files, single .eml messages, mailbox files without an extension (Thunderbird's Inbox , say), and Maildir folders: open a Maildir with "Open as mailbox". You get threads or a plain message list, a filter by sender and subject, unread, flagged, replied and forwarded marks, and a folder list for a mailbox with sub-mailboxes. Attachments are listed and download with a click; images among them show inline. A message that only has an HTML version is shown as plain text: nothing in it is loaded or run. Very large mailboxes thread their first 250,000 messages.

A database dump ( .sql , .mysql , .pgsql , .dump , also compressed with gzip, bzip2, xz or zstd) opens as its schema: which program made it, from which server and database, and when, then every table with its row count, data size, columns, keys, indexes and foreign keys, plus views, triggers and routines. It reads dumps from mysqldump and MariaDB, phpMyAdmin, Adminer and HeidiSQL, PostgreSQL's pg_dump (plain format), SQLite's .dump , and plain SQL scripts. It shows the structure and counts, not the rows; the SQL tab shows the text itself. A dump that looks cut off says so.

Disk images open read-only, without mounting anything: raw images ( .img , .dd , .raw , .bin ), ISO discs, VHD, VHDX, VMDK, VDI, qcow and Apple disk images ( .dmg ). BackDown shows the partition table and names each partition's file system (NTFS, exFAT, FAT, ext2/3/4, XFS, btrfs, APFS, HFS+ and more, with BitLocker and LUKS shown as encrypted). The files inside can be browsed on FAT, exFAT, ext2/3/4 and NTFS partitions, and on ISO discs, in raw images, fixed-size VHD and fixed-size VDI. Files inside open in the same viewers and can be downloaded, and deleted files on FAT, exFAT and NTFS can be listed and copied out ( Recover deleted files ). For the other formats (VMDK, VHDX, qcow, and growing VHD and VDI images), convert to a raw image first, for example with qemu-img convert -O raw . BackDown can't browse the files in .dmg images itself. When an image holds file systems BackDown doesn't read itself (XFS, btrfs, HFS+, APFS and others), the viewer offers Mount read-only : the system attaches the image read-only and mounts what it can read (udisks on Linux, hdiutil on macOS; on Windows, only ISO, VHD and VHDX images). Each mounted file system then has Index this , and Detach unmounts it and lets the image go. backdown mount does the same in a terminal ( mounting drives ).
Drives on another machine are listed under Machines in the sidebar and browse the same way, read-only, with each file's copies here and there. Their files don't open or preview here.

The browser listens on this computer only, unless you ask. --host ADDRESS makes it listen on one more address as well, such as this computer's Tailscale address, so you can look at your drives from your phone or another computer: backdown serve --host 100.x.y.z Copy BackDown browser for /home/you/.local/share/backdown/index.db at http://127.0.0.1:8787/?t=4f0c… and from other devices, to look but not change anything, at http://100.x.y.z:8787/?t=4f0c… (the link carries a one-time token; Ctrl-C to stop) Copy From anywhere but this computer, BackDown only shows what's there. Browsing, the time slider, search, the viewers and downloading a copy of a file work, and so does asking for a rescan. Nothing can be wiped, copied, rescued, mounted, opened with a program or otherwise changed, and settings stay as they are: "Over the network, BackDown only shows what's there: freeing up drives, copying, rescuing, mounting, opening files and changing settings need someone at the computer BackDown runs on." The link's token is still needed, as on this computer. 127.0.0.1 keeps listening, so backdown app and backdown open work as before. The link works with the address you gave, with this computer's full Tailscale name ( nextcloud.tailnet-1234.ts.net , when Tailscale runs here; from v1.0.0-beta.2, the next release) and, on Linux, with its short name. Other names it's reached by (your own DNS, a reverse proxy) can be allowed with BACKDOWN_HOST_NAMES=name1,name2 (also from beta.2). The connection is plain HTTP. Over Tailscale the network encrypts it; on any other network, someone who can watch it could read the token and what you look at. Prefer an address only your own devices can reach: a wildcard such as 0.0.0.0 listens on every network the computer is on. For the background service: backdown daemon --host 100.x.y.z , or, on Linux, backdown service install --host 100.x.y.z . From beta.2, backdown token --links prints its links with the token in them (before that, the token is in ui.json in your data folder ): one for this computer and one for your other devices, named by Tailscale when it can be. backdown token prints the token alone. On macOS and Windows, service install doesn't pass --host on to the service yet, and the machine-wide service on Linux stays cut off from the network by systemd.

Browsing never writes to your drives. Everything that changes something (copying into an archive, freeing up a drive, rescuing, rescanning) happens in the background service and is described in its own guide. The browser opened with backdown serve can't do those; it says which command to run instead. The viewers for databases, spreadsheets, presentations, mailboxes and SQL dumps are marked Pro; in this beta everything is unlocked ( Free and Pro ).

The Settings view, how often drives are rescanned, updates, notifications, running BackDown for the whole machine, and what's free and what's Pro. Most of what you can change is in the Settings view, at the bottom of the sidebar. The background service reads it as it goes: a change applies from the next scan, hash, plan or check, without a restart. Some of it can also be given as options on the command line, for one run.

The index is one SQLite database, index.db , in your BackDown data folder: System Data folder Linux ~/.local/share/backdown (or $XDG_DATA_HOME/backdown ) macOS ~/Library/Application Support/BackDown Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\BackDown Linux, machine-wide service /var/lib/backdown The folder is readable only by you: the index lists every file path on your drives. backdown status and Settings > Index and data show which index is in use. There's no setting that moves it; to use another one, pass --db to any command, or set BACKDOWN_DB : backdown --db /media/archive/backdown/index.db status export BACKDOWN_DB=/media/archive/backdown/index.db Copy To move it for good: stop the background service, move index.db (with index.db-wal and index.db-shm if they're there), then set BACKDOWN_DB where the service starts, or pass --db . Previews before 0.2.0-alpha.3 kept backdown.db in the current folder. BackDown mentions it if it finds one; keep using it with --db backdown.db , or index again.

The service rescans each drive every 24 hours, and as soon as a drive that was away comes back, whatever the setting says. In Settings > Scanning, "Rescan each drive" can be every 6 or 12 hours, every day, every 3 days, every week, or "Only when I ask, or a drive comes back". It applies straight away. backdown daemon --rescan-every 12h (or 30m , 7d , never ) sets it when the service starts; a change in Settings then applies until the service starts again with that option. --port moves the browser from port 8787. Under "Fast rescans" in the same section: Use the drive's change log and file table when possible (on): off, every scan walks every folder. Walk every folder anyway, every 10 scans , or when the last walk is 30 days old : 0 turns either reason off. Fast rescans explains what these do, and backdown index --method walk walks whatever they say.

"Readers per drive" (1 to 16) is how many files are read at once from each drive for the hashing after each scan: 1 suits spinning disks, 2 to 4 suit SSDs. It's --jobs for backdown hash . "After each scan, try again files that couldn't be read before" is backdown hash --retry-errors , every time. Junk rules decide which folders count as regenerable : caches, thumbnails, node_modules , trash and the like. Settings lists the built-in ones; under "Also count these folder names" you can add your own, one name per line (a name, not a path; case doesn't matter). They count from the next time drives are recognised: after a scan, or What's here > Recognise again. They apply to the command line too.

The service keeps a list of what's worth knowing: a drive whose health got worse, a mirror that no longer matches what it copies, a job it scheduled itself that failed (a scan, hashing, a sync). It's under Notifications in the Activity view, with read and unread, and a count on the Activity button. In Settings > Notifications: Show notifications on the desktop turns the pop-ups on or off; everything is listed in Activity either way. The same switch is "Show on the desktop" in Activity. When a drive's health gets worse , When a mirror no longer matches what it copies , When a scheduled job fails choose which kinds pop up. Every kind is listed in Activity either way, so a failing drive is never missed. Send a test notification checks that pop-ups work. At most 3 pop-ups show in any 10 minutes and 12 a day; the rest are listed only ("listed only" beside them). A drive that's failing always gets through, if pop-ups are on. The same notice isn't repeated for a while: 7 days for a drive's verdict, 20 hours for the rest. Pop-ups use notify-send on Linux (or the desktop's notification service), Notification Center on macOS, and a PowerShell notification on Windows, where Windows may name PowerShell as the sender. The machine-wide service doesn't pop anything up: it isn't on anyone's desktop.

BackDown makes no network requests unless you ask, so it doesn't look for updates until you tell it to: Check now in Settings > Updates, or backdown update --check , asks once. --check exits with 10 when there's a newer version. Look for updates once a day makes the background service ask once a day. Updates to offer : "Automatic" offers previews while you're running a preview (like this beta) and releases otherwise; "Releases only" or "Previews too" fix it ( --channel stable|preview ). What it asks is GitHub's public list of BackDown releases; nothing about you, your drives or your files is sent. The answer is kept for a day ( update.json in your data folder); --refresh asks again. When there's a newer version, the browser shows a banner with the release notes and Update now . backdown update --check backdown update backdown update --rollback Copy Installing downloads this computer's archive and the release's SHA256SUMS.txt over HTTPS, and refuses unless the archive's SHA-256 matches. It unpacks the new program beside the one you have, checks that it runs and says the expected version, keeps a copy of the old one in your data folder ( previous/ ), swaps them, and restarts the background service. If the new one doesn't start, the old one is put back. --rollback puts back the version the last update replaced. The sums come from the same release as the download, so they prove the file arrived whole and is the one published there; they aren't a signature. Some copies of BackDown are updated another way, and backdown update (or How to update in the browser) says so instead of installing: installed from the .deb (it lives in /usr/bin ) or another package: install the new package; an AppImage: download the new AppImage; BackDown.app on a Mac (from the .dmg ): download the new .dmg , since changing the program inside the app would break its signature; installed from the .msi on Windows: install the new .msi , which upgrades the one you have (the setup .zip install updates itself); Homebrew: brew upgrade backdown ; in a folder you can't write to: sudo backdown update , or move it somewhere you own; the machine-wide service: sudo backdown update , then sudo systemctl restart backdown .

On a NAS or a Linux server, one daemon can index the whole machine for everyone: sudo mv backdown /usr/local/bin/ sudo backdown service install --system sudo usermod -aG backdown alice Copy It runs as a backdown user that can read every file and write none, with the whole file system read-only to it except its own folder, /var/lib/backdown , and no network beyond this computer, all enforced by systemd. Members of the backdown group can use it with the usual commands and backdown open (after logging in again). It only reads: it doesn't wipe, rescue, tidy, mount, reach other machines or check for updates. Do those from your own account with --local . It's Linux-only; on macOS and Windows the service runs while you're logged in. backdown service status (with --system for this one) says whether it's installed and running and what it's doing; backdown service uninstall removes it and keeps the index.

System What backdown service install sets up Its messages Linux a systemd user service, ~/.config/systemd/user/backdown.service journalctl --user -u backdown macOS a LaunchAgent, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.backdown.daemon.plist , started at login and restarted if it stops unexpectedly ~/Library/Logs/BackDown/daemon.log Windows a scheduled task "BackDown" that starts it, without a window, when you log on (not elevated), restarted if it fails none kept yet On Linux, to start it with other options, override its command with a systemd drop-in: systemctl --user edit backdown Copy [Service] ExecStart= ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backdown daemon --rescan-every 12h Copy Then systemctl --user restart backdown . backdown service install --print shows the unit it installs. To keep the user service running while you're logged out, loginctl enable-linger $USER . Most options are in Settings anyway, which is simpler.

Command What it does index Index every file under each PATH as a new scan (read-only; re-run to update). hash Hash only what could be a duplicate: size, then a sample, then full SHA-256. dupes List duplicated content, largest reclaimable space first (runs hash first). check Is PATH safe to wipe? Every file needs a SHA-256-identical copy outside PATH (runs hash first). Exits 0 when safe, 2 when files must be copied first. import-legacy Import the index the pre-Rust scripts wrote (bd-index.sh, bd-hash.py), so their crawling and hashing aren't repeated. volumes Every disk and partition on this machine: what's on it, and what BackDown can do with it (read-only; needs no root). health How each drive is doing: SMART verdict, temperature, bad sectors, wear, and what changed since its first reading (read now, without root; kept in the index). Exits 2 when a connected drive is failing. mount Mount a partition read-only (one backdown volumes calls mountable), or attach a disk image read-only and mount what's on it; never read-write, and as you: udisks on Linux, diskutil and hdiutil on macOS (Windows attaches ISO, VHD and VHDX images). Install it (verified against the release's SHA-256 sums). service Run the daemon as a service (systemd on Linux, a login item on macOS, a task at logon on Windows): install, uninstall or check it. entities What things are: mail stores, backups, phones, systems, repositories, libraries… with where they came from (reads small files like backup scripts on connected drives). overlaps How much of each drive, folder and recognised thing already exists elsewhere, and where. report The whole picture as a document: drives, what's on them, overlaps, duplicates, and which drives are safe to wipe. plan Propose where everything on the old drives goes in one archive, and why (saved, so it can be applied). plans Plans made so far. apply Apply a plan: show what it would do, or with --go copy, verify and journal every file (never deletes anything). rescue Get files back from a failing, formatted or emptied drive or card (only reads it). mirror Keep a folder (usually part of the archive) copied on another drive, and check the copy now and then. wipe Free drives (or folders on them): delete only what has a verified copy elsewhere, moving what exists only here to --move-to first. Both files are re-read first; every link is journaled. Without --go, only shows what would happen. mail Mailboxes: merge copies of one into a single Maildir, or export a Maildir folder as mbox.

Every command takes these. --db <DB> Index database (default: your BackDown data folder; see backdown status ). Also read from $BACKDOWN_DB . --local Work on the index directly even if a BackDown daemon is running. -h , --help Print help ( --help shows more than -h ). -V , --version Print the version.

When the daemon is running, it owns the index: index , hash , dupes , check , scans , status , health , remote sync and apply --go are handed to it and you follow its progress in the terminal; wipe , dedup --go and mail merge check first, then hand the work to it. Everything else reads the index directly. --local makes any command work on the index itself instead. import-legacy refuses to write while a daemon is running: stop it first. On Windows, commands always use the index directly.

Code Meaning 0 Done. For check : safe to wipe. 1 Something went wrong; the message says what. license show : no licence. In a release version, a Pro command without a licence. 2 Finished, with a result to act on: check found files that exist nowhere else (or couldn't be read); apply , wipe , mirror sync , mirror verify , dedup or mail merge had conflicts, failures or mismatches; health found a connected drive failing; rescue image couldn't read everything; rescue find or rescue partitions found nothing. 3 service status : the service isn't running. 10 update --check : there's a newer version.

BACKDOWN_BROWSER The Chromium-family browser backdown app uses, like --browser . BACKDOWN_NO_UPDATE_CHECK When set, the daemon never looks for updates, whatever Settings says. XDG_DATA_HOME , XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (Linux) Where the data folder and the daemon's socket go: $XDG_DATA_HOME/backdown (default ~/.local/share/backdown ) and $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/backdown . LOCALAPPDATA (Windows) The data folder is %LOCALAPPDATA%\BackDown .
Index every file under each PATH as a new scan (read-only; re-run to update). backdown index [OPTIONS] <PATHS>... Copy
<PATHS>... The drives or folders to index, each as its own root. Roots can't be nested: index each drive or top-level folder once.

--cross-filesystems Also descend into other filesystems mounted below PATH. --allow-empty Record PATH even if it's now empty although it held files (normally refused: an empty mount point usually means the drive is unplugged). --method <METHOD> How to find what's there: auto (the drive's change log if it's intact, else NTFS's file table where the device can be read, else a walk; and a walk every so often), walk (every folder), journal or table (that way or fail, saying why). Default: auto . One of auto , walk , journal , table . Also takes the global options --db and --local .

A drive that is suddenly empty although its last scan held files (usually an unplugged drive's leftover mount point) is refused and nothing is recorded; pass --allow-empty if it really was emptied. Symbolic links are not followed. When a daemon is running, the scan is handed to it and it hashes the new files next. With --method auto , a rescan reads the drive's change log where there is one (the USN journal of NTFS drives on Windows, the change history of APFS and HFS+ drives on macOS), or NTFS's file table (on Windows as administrator, on Linux for ntfs-3g mounts whose device your account can read), and walks every folder whenever either can't vouch for every file, and anyway every tenth scan or after 30 days (Settings > Scanning). Linux keeps no change log for drives. Each drive's line says how it was scanned and, for a walk, why. --method journal or table stops with the reason instead of walking.
backdown index /media/old-drive /media/archive # a NAS share with other file systems mounted inside it backdown index /mnt/nas --cross-filesystems # Windows backdown index E:\ F:\Archive Copy

<PATH> The drive or folder to check. It must be there now (connected and mounted).

--list List the files that have no copy elsewhere (the largest 20,000). --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. --jobs <JOBS> Readers per device; 1 suits spinning disks, raise it for SSDs. Default: 1 . --retry-errors Retry files that failed to read last time. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Exits 0 when every file has a SHA-256-identical copy outside PATH ("SAFE TO WIPE"), and 2 when some files exist nowhere else or couldn't be read ("COPY FIRST"). Copies on drives that aren't connected still count: the verdict is about the index. --list lists the largest 20,000 such files. Empty files don't count against a drive.

Import the index the pre-Rust scripts wrote (bd-index.sh, bd-hash.py), so their crawling and hashing aren't repeated. backdown import-legacy [OPTIONS] <INDEX_DIR> Copy

--hashes <HASHES_DB> bd-hash.py's hashes.db: attach its SHA-256s to the files they belong to. --map <LEGACY=NOW> A drive mounted somewhere else now: LEGACY_PATH=PATH_NOW (repeatable; a legacy folder maps everything below it). --volume <NAME> Import only this volume, a folder name in INDEX_DIR (repeatable; default: all). --replace Replace what the index already holds for a root, or for roots nested with it. --dry-run Read everything and show what would be imported, writing nothing. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

The legacy index is the `index` folder the pre-Rust scripts wrote: <vol>/chunks.list bd-plan.py's crawl plan, one `R<TAB>dir` or `F<TAB>dir` per line; its first line, `F<TAB>/mount/point`, names the drive's root <vol>/chunks/<id>.tsv one chunk, from `find -printf '%s\t%T@\t%p\n'`: size, mtime (seconds.fraction) and the raw path; <id>.done marks it finished <vol>.tsv every finished chunk, merged (read when present and up to date) hashes.db bd-hash.py's table h(path, size, mtime, sha256) Each volume becomes a root with one finished scan, dated from its chunks. Chunks that never finished are left out and counted; the next `backdown index` adds their files. A hash attaches where the path, size and mtime (to the second) still match. Safe to run again: an interrupted import resumes, a finished one is left alone. Stop the daemon while importing. Afterwards `dupes` and `check` work straight away, and `backdown index <root>` with the drive mounted finds its files unchanged and keeps their hashes. Examples: backdown import-legacy ~/scripts/index --hashes ~/scripts/index/hashes.db --dry-run backdown import-legacy ~/scripts/index --hashes ~/scripts/index/hashes.db \ --map /media/olduser/Photos=/mnt/photos Copy
Every disk and partition on this machine: what's on it, and what BackDown can do with it (read-only; needs no root). backdown volumes [OPTIONS] Copy
--json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Reads sysfs, udev and mountinfo on Linux, diskutil on macOS and the storage cmdlets on Windows. It never mounts or writes anything, says what BackDown can do with each partition (mountable, mounted, system, encrypted, part of a volume group, swap, empty), and marks the volumes an existing index covers.

How each drive is doing: SMART verdict, temperature, bad sectors, wear, and what changed since its first reading (read now, without root; kept in the index). Exits 2 when a connected drive is failing. backdown health [OPTIONS] Copy
--json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Reads each drive's own health reports (SMART) as you, without administrator rights: through udisks (and smartctl where your account may use it) on Linux, diskutil (and smartctl , if installed) on macOS, and the storage cmdlets on Windows, which share error counters only with an administrator. smartctl is asked not to wake a drive that has spun down. What can't be read is noted, with the command that would read it. Readings are kept in the index under the drive's serial number, so its history follows it from port to port. When the daemon runs (Linux and macOS), health has it read every drive now; it also reads them every six hours, when a drive appears and when an indexed drive comes back. No self-tests are run. Exits 2 when a connected drive is failing.
backdown health # in a script: 2 = a connected drive is failing backdown health --json > health.json Copy

--port <PORT> Port to listen on. Default: 8787 . --host <HOST> Also listen on this address (e.g. this computer's Tailscale IP) so other devices can look; from there BackDown only shows, and changes need this computer. 127.0.0.1 always listens. Default: 127.0.0.1 . --no-open Don't open a browser, just print the link. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

The browser listens on 127.0.0.1 and prints a private link with a one-time token. It only reads: copying, wiping, rescues and rescans need the background service ( backdown app , or backdown service install then backdown open ). --host ADDRESS also listens on that address, a Tailscale address such as 100.x.y.z say, and prints the link to use from your other devices. From anywhere but this computer, BackDown only shows what's there: nothing can be wiped, copied, rescued, mounted, opened or changed, and the link's token is still needed. A wildcard such as 0.0.0.0 listens on every address, 127.0.0.1 included.

Run in the background: rescan drives, hash, serve the web UI. Usually started by backdown service install rather than by hand. backdown daemon [OPTIONS] Copy

One job at a time (scan, hash, recognise, copy, mirror, wipe, tidy, mail merge), so the index has a single writer and each drive a single reader; rescues and syncs with other machines run beside them, and drive health is read every six hours. Every copy is written beside its destination under a temporary name, read back and compared before it takes its name. A name the archive's drive would take for another, or can't hold, is copied under another name ( photo (2).jpg ) and journaled; extended attributes (macOS) and alternate data streams (Windows) are copied, and what couldn't be kept is listed. Free drives (or folders on them): delete only what has a verified copy elsewhere, moving what exists only here to --move-to first. Without --go, only shows what would happen. backdown wipe [OPTIONS] <PATHS>... Copy
<PATHS>... Drives, or folders on them, to free. Each must be on an indexed drive.

--move-to <MOVE_TO> Move what exists only in these paths here first (verified), instead of leaving it. --trust-index Don't re-read each file and its copy; trust the index's hashes (faster, a little less safe). Copies must still be there, as last scanned. --go Actually wipe. --confirm <CONFIRM> The drive name(s), as the dry run shows them. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Refuses the running system (outside home folders), a whole home folder, BackDown's own index, and anything not on an indexed drive. Each file is re-read before it's deleted, and so is its copy outside the selection; --trust-index checks only that the copy is still there as last scanned. Changed, new or unreadable files are left alone. Every deletion is journaled with its proof. Folders the wipe empties are removed (a drive's own top folder stays). A copy only on another machine ( backdown remote ) counts when that machine confirmed it within the proof window, and is read again there just before the deletion. --move-to keeps names as they are, and leaves a file in place if its extended attributes or alternate data streams couldn't be kept on the copy.

Tidy an archive: identical files in FOLDER share their storage, as hardlinks or clones. Both files are re-read first; every link is journaled. Without --go, only shows what would happen. backdown dedup [OPTIONS] <FOLDER> Copy
<FOLDER> The folder to tidy, usually the archive. Only files inside it, on the same drive, are linked.

--link <LINK> hard: one file with several names (any filesystem; editing one edits them all). clone: separate files sharing blocks until one changes (btrfs, XFS, APFS). Default: hard . --min-size <MIN_SIZE> Leave smaller files alone (e.g. 4K, 1M). Default: 4K . --dry-run Only show what would happen (the default). --go Link them. --json Print it as JSON, for scripts. Also takes the global options --db and --local .

Only files the index has hashed and that are identical, on the same drive, inside FOLDER; files whose permissions, owner or extended attributes differ (and, for hardlinks, their modification time), or that also have names outside FOLDER, are left alone. Clones need btrfs, XFS or APFS. Each pair is read again first; every link is journaled, and running it again carries on. It refuses the running system, whole home folders and BackDown's index, and isn't available on Windows yet. Index the drive afterwards (the daemon does). Exits 2 when some files failed.

The sources are only read. backdown mail merge [OPTIONS] --to <TO> <SOURCES>... Copy Arguments <SOURCES>... The copies of the mailbox: Maildirs, mbox files, Thunderbird account folders, or whole mail stores (folders of Maildirs), in any order. They are only read. Options --to <TO> The merged Maildir: a new folder (running again carries on where it stopped). --dry-run Read everything and show what the merge would be, writing nothing. --json Print it as JSON, for scripts.
